title: "Self-Prep"
subtitle: "Two notebook series that take a topic from zero to job-ready — and show their working."

---

Every notebook here does the same thing: build one topic up from nothing, implement it from
scratch, break it on purpose, and then say plainly what it is bad at.

The rule that shapes all of them is that **no claim is made that was not measured**. Every code
cell has been executed in order with warnings treated as errors, and every number quoted in the
prose was checked against what the code actually printed. Where a result contradicted the point
being made, the prose was rewritten to match the result — those cases are flagged where they
occur, and they are usually the most useful parts.

::: {.grid}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### [ML: Zero to Hero](ML-Zero-to-Hero/index.qmd)

**16 notebooks · complete · 952 cells**

Foundations, then the models, then the cross-cutting problems, then the applied ones. Each
notebook implements the algorithm from scratch, checks it against scikit-learn in the same cell,
and spends a full section on the thing that most often goes wrong.

A few of the results it argues for:

- A random train/test split inflates a time-series score by 28% — measured, not asserted.
- Resampling before the split fabricates a 0.83 ROC-AUC out of pure noise.
- The best-RMSE recommender is nearly the worst recommender.
- LOF scores *below random* on real card fraud — and there is a one-parameter fix.

[Start with NB-00 →](ML-Zero-to-Hero/ml_foundations_zero_to_hero.ipynb)
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### [DSA: Zero to Hero](DSA-Zero-to-Hero/index.qmd)

**23 notebooks · 9 built · in progress**

The same treatment for data structures and algorithms, with a stricter quality bar — because in
this domain correctness and cost are decidable, so they get tested rather than asserted:

- Every implementation stress-tested against a brute-force reference.
- **Python and Java written side by side** and checked against each other on identical inputs.
- Every complexity **measured** at doubling sizes, not claimed.
- Every invariant asserted in code after every operation.

[**NB-00 Complexity & Amortised Analysis**](DSA-Zero-to-Hero/complexity_zero_to_hero.ipynb)
builds the harness the other 22 notebooks import, and finds a measurement whose verdict changes
between runs. [**NB-01 Arrays**](DSA-Zero-to-Hero/arrays_zero_to_hero.ipynb) prices the dynamic
array's growth factor as a trade. [**NB-02 Strings**](DSA-Zero-to-Hero/strings_zero_to_hero.ipynb)
takes the best-known piece of string folklore and finds it wrong in a second way nobody mentions:
CPython's `+=` optimisation fails on size as well as on aliasing, so the same loop is exactly
linear under a megabyte and exactly quadratic above it.
[**NB-03 Hashing**](DSA-Zero-to-Hero/hashing_zero_to_hero.ipynb) constructs the input that turns a
`dict` quadratic, and shows Python and Java each defending the axis the other leaves open.
[**NB-04 Linked Lists**](DSA-Zero-to-Hero/linked_lists_zero_to_hero.ipynb) builds the structure and
then makes the measured case against it.
[**NB-05 Stacks, Queues & Deques**](DSA-Zero-to-Hero/stacks_queues_zero_to_hero.ipynb) builds the
circular buffer, counts an amortised bound exactly, and derives the monotonic stack from an
invariant it asserts in the loop.
[**NB-06 Trees & Traversals**](DSA-Zero-to-Hero/trees_zero_to_hero.ipynb) measures the recursion
limit precisely enough to kill the folk rule about it.
[**NB-07 Binary Search Trees**](DSA-Zero-to-Hero/bst_zero_to_hero.ipynb) adds the ordering
invariant and measures what happens when nothing enforces balance.
[**NB-08 Balanced Trees & B-Trees**](DSA-Zero-to-Hero/balanced_trees_zero_to_hero.ipynb) is the
answer, and the first structure in the series whose guarantee holds whatever the input does.

[Start with NB-00 →](DSA-Zero-to-Hero/complexity_zero_to_hero.ipynb) ·
[Read the plan →](DSA-Zero-to-Hero/plan.qmd)
:::

## How each notebook is laid out

The same seven parts every time, so you always know where to look.

| Part | Contents |
|------|----------|
| **0** | Setup — one install cell, one import cell |
| **1** | **Theory from zero** — numbered steps, implemented from scratch, checked against a reference in the same cell |
| **2** | **Worked example** — one problem, end to end, nothing skipped |
| **3** | The topic's signature difficulty, in depth |
| **4** | **Tough questions** — ~12 with hidden answers, plus 3 coding challenges |
| **5** | **Practice** — 5–10 datasets or problems, each with a brief and the trap it sets |
| **6** | **Reading** — the papers behind each section, with an "if you read only one" pick |

## Running them yourself

Everything is plain Jupyter. Clone the repo and open any notebook:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/abpanic/Self-Prep.git
pip install numpy pandas matplotlib scipy scikit-learn
```

Each notebook's Part 0 installs anything else it needs, so opening one and running it top to
bottom is enough. A few practice datasets download from OpenML on first use and cache afterwards.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why some code cells show no output

Nine of the sixteen ML notebooks are currently stored without their execution outputs, so on this
site their code appears with no results beneath it. Every one of them passes a full top-to-bottom
run under warnings-as-errors — the outputs simply have not been saved back into the files yet.
Run them locally and you will see everything the prose describes.
